To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
different sitting postures result in changes in cervical posture, and that lumbar and pelvic posture should be considered when attempting to control cervical posture.
different sitting postures result in changes in head, neck, and lumbar position.
the head, cervical spine, and pelvis are affected differently by different sitting positions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of lumbar posture on cervical posture.
the influence of lumbar and pelvic posture on cervical posture during sitting and we have shown that there is a relationship between lumbar and cervical posture during different sitting positions.
the effects of sitting posture on spinal alignment and how this may influence the development of low back pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lumbar position influences the cervical position, but the relationship is not straightforward.
the cervical spine adjusts to maintain a neutral position in response to changes in lumbar and pelvic posture.
the lumbar spine and pelvis do influence the position of the head, neck, and upper cervical spine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lumbar and cervical spine are linked and the position of one is related to the position of the other.
the head, neck, and lumbar spine are linked in a complex relationship.
the lumbar spine has a significant impact on cervical position.
The main takeaway from our work is that
lumbar posture can be manipulated to change cervical spine posture and this can be used in a rehabilitation program.
lumbar posture is associated with changes in overall cervical posture and this association is primarily mediated through compensatory adjustments in the upper cervical spine.
the lumbar and pelvic postures are very important in the cervical spine.
